question.problem:
In a math test, a student has a $55%$ probability of correctly answering each question. Using the normal approximation to the binomial distribution, estimate the probability that a student correctly solves more than $10$ questions of a $20$-question test. Give your final answer to three decimal places.

*Hint: The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z)$ for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-0.4\,$ | $\,0.3446\,$ | $\,0.3409\,$ | $\,0.3372\,$ |
| $\,-0.3\,$ | $\,0.3821\,$ | $\,0.3783\,$ | $\,0.3745\,$ |
| $\,-0.2\,$ | $\,0.4207\,$ | $\,0.4168\,$ | $\,0.4129\,$ |
question.worked_solution:
Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=20$ and $p=0.55.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =20\cdot 0.55 \\  & =11 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =20\cdot (1-0.55) \\  & =9 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(20)(0.55)=11
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(20)(0.55)(1-0.55)=4.95.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(11,4.95).$

Now, we can estimate the desired probability $P(X>10).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(X>10)=P(X\ge 11)≈P(Y\ge 10.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\ge 10.5) & =P(Z\ge \frac{10.5-11}{\sqrt{4.95}}) \\  & ≈P(Z\ge -0.22) \\  & =1-P(Z<-0.22) \\  & =1-P(Z\le -0.22) \\  & =1-Φ(-0.22) \\  & =1-0.4129 \\  & =0.5871\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(X>10)≈0.587.
$$

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.5914.$
